json.text:
The Association posted the reinspection notice for Mapo Gate 3 at 9:20 a.m., and by 9:40 Do-yoon knew he had broken something.

He read it twice on the hall's public board. *Gate MP-003 — grade under review. Entry suspended pending survey.* Eleven cores, nine of them two grades above envelope, and a clerk who had done her job properly at 7:40 the previous morning.

The first time, nobody had flagged Mapo Gate 3. The first time, there had been no anomalous cores, because the eleventh core had been pulled out of a chamber nobody entered — the chamber that had come down on Park Mu-jin's leg and ended his walking, and with it the run, and with it the count.

Do-yoon had kept an old man's leg. In exchange, the Association was now looking at a gate that should have gone unwatched for another five months.

*It isn't the same river.*

He had told himself for eleven days that his memory was a map. Standing in front of the board he understood that it was a map of a country he had already begun to demolish.

“You're the porter.”

The woman had come up on his left without any of the noise a person normally makes. Association jacket, no rank pin, a tablet held the way people hold a thing they have already finished reading.

“I'm a porter,” Do-yoon said.

“You're the porter who told Park Mu-jin to take the right corridor.” She did not look up from the tablet. “Yoon Ha-eun. Survey division. I have his statement, the team lead's statement, and eleven cores that don't belong in a D-gate.” Now she looked up. “I don't have yours.”

“He asked me for a reason. I gave him a reason.”

“You gave him a third chamber.” She let that sit. “The survey filed nine days before your run counts two. I walked it myself this morning. There are three.”

Do-yoon kept his face still, which was itself a kind of answer, and he knew it.

“Then the survey was wrong,” he said.

“The survey was wrong,” Ha-eun agreed. “That's the part that interests my division. Surveys are wrong about corridors. They are not wrong about rooms.” She tapped the tablet once against her palm. “An F-rank porter walked into a gate he had never entered and corrected a filed survey. Either you have a source inside my division, Mister Kang, or you have something my division doesn't have a form for.”

“I have a bad feeling about ceilings.”

“Mm.” It was not a laugh. “Mu-jin said you'd say something like that.”

claims.statement: Mapo Gate 3 is suspended pending a reinspection after the anomalous cores.
The survey division questions Do-yoon about his knowledge of the third chamber.

json.text:
Mu-jin was in the yard behind the hall, sitting on a crate with his left leg stretched out straight in front of him, the way a man sits when the leg is fine and he has been thinking about it anyway.

“Eighteen percent,” he said, without turning. “Still eighteen. She didn't ask me to take it back.”

“She asked you about me.”

“She asked me everything about you. Where you were from, who trained you, what you ate.” He shifted the leg. “I told her the truth, which is that I don't know any of it, and that you were eleven minutes early.”

Do-yoon sat down on the next crate. Four hunters crossed the yard toward the gate lists. None of them looked at a pair of porters.

“Mister Park. The gate's suspended.”

“I can read.”

“The reinspection was because of the cores. The cores were high because we took the right corridor.” He said it carefully, laying it down the way you lay something down in front of a man who is allowed to pick it up or not. “If we had gone left, the ceiling comes down, the third chamber empties into the first, and nobody ever counts what was in it. The gate stays a D-gate on paper for months.”

Mu-jin was quiet long enough for someone across the yard to shout a name that was not theirs.

“You're telling me the gate got flagged because I lived.”

“I'm telling you the gate got flagged because the third chamber stayed dry.”

“That's the same sentence with the blood wiped off it.” He pulled out the cigarette he had not lit inside the gate yesterday and turned it over between two fingers. “Say the rest.”

“There is no rest.”

“Kid.” Mu-jin finally looked at him. “Yesterday you knew about a room in a gate you had never been inside. Today you know why a reinspection happened before the survey division does. I'm old. I'm not stupid. And I'm not asking.” He put the cigarette away. “I'm telling you that whatever it is, it moves things. You should have worked that out before you opened your mouth in that corridor.”

“I did work it out.”

“And?”

“I'd rather have you than the gate.”

Mu-jin made a sound that was not a word, and looked out at the yard for a while.

“Eighteen percent,” he said again. “Association's going to run that survey Thursday. They'll want a porter who's been inside. That's you now, and that's not a favor.”

Do-yoon thought about Thursday, and found nothing there. Nothing at all: no shape, no rumor, no remembered headline. The first time, Thursday had been a day he spent carrying water filters in Guro.

He had eleven days of future left that he trusted, and he had just spent one of them on an old man's leg.

Across the yard, Yoon Ha-eun stood at the hall door with her tablet against her hip, watching the two of them the way a surveyor watches a ceiling.

json.summary_l1: The morning after the Mapo run. The Association suspends Gate 3 pending reinspection because of the anomalous cores, and Do-yoon realises his own success changed a future he was relying on. A survey-division officer questions him about the third chamber and he gives her nothing. In the yard Mu-jin presses him directly, is refused, and keeps him at eighteen percent anyway. Do-yoon reaches for Thursday and finds no memory of it at all.
